title: Controller Semantics and Negative Results in a Synthetic Cross-Layer Orchestration Study — bounded reproducibility evidence
abstract: Digital-twin context can guide network and computation choices, but a controller label does not establish information equivalence, meaningful optimization, or improved service. This article audits two preserved synthetic cross-layer orchestration implementations and their negative results. In the original five-seed held-out study, the procedural twin policy underperforms cloud fallback by 0.01360 utility units, with a post hoc paired 95% interval [-0.01478,-0.01242]. A separately reproduced revision retains a negative difference of 0.01255 and unfavorable adaptive-fidelity and checkpoint outcomes. Source inequalities show that the full linear selector chooses edge placement on the available path with the smallest configured penalty; focused assertions confirm this behavior on 9,600 reconstructed input states in each version, separately. A zero-latency transformation instead creates score ties. The symmetric SLSQP share objective has a uniform mathematical optimum, but optimizes a different function from network/placement utility and returns small budget residuals. A bounded numerical analysis finds these residuals too small to reverse the retained negative comparisons. Switching accounting, incomplete action feasibility, unequal consumed information/computation, and truth-changing interventions limit causal interpretation. The contribution is a reproducible methodological characterization of this model, with no measured network, general adaptive superiority, or established novelty claim.
